source.title: Revisiting Small Batch Training for Deep Neural Networks

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how mini-batch size affects test performance and training stability under a fixed epoch budget, using a broad sweep of batch sizes and learning rates. It does not reproduce the original large-batch experiments exactly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own batch-size experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Results cited from prior work, including Hoffer et al. and Goyal et al., are not recorded as rows. Figure-only curves are recorded without reconstructing numerical values.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests V5 by varying SGD mini-batch size and measuring held-out accuracy at fixed epoch budgets, as in the original large-batch experiments. Its learning-rate parameterization is equivalent to linear scaling, and learning rates are swept separately for each batch size. It is not an original source of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that small batches deliver the best held-out performance and training stability for a fixed number of epochs in their experiments. Warm-up and longer training improve large-batch results without fully recovering small-batch performance. Useful batch sizes depend on normalization and dataset, with ImageNet optima reported at 16–64. Their computational-cost comparison counts gradient calculations rather than elapsed hardware time.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares mini-batch sizes using standard SGD and held epoch budgets, but uses its own learning-rate formulation and sweeps a broad range of base learning rates; it does not reproduce a single prior large-batch recipe. It tests image classifiers only.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with dataset, architecture, batch normalization, data augmentation, learning rate, warm-up, training length, and the distinction between overall SGD batch size and BN batch size.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed base learning rate, larger batches can degrade training convergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mini-batch size affects optimization convergence under linearly scaled learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing batch size narrows the range of base learning rates permitting stable convergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger SGD batches reduce robustness to the choice of learning rate.

record.problems: Most performance curves are figure-only and exact test values cannot be recovered from the text. ImageNet results average two runs; most other results do not report uncertainty or multiple-run statistics. The experiments cover image classifiers and selected architectures, not language models. Momentum was omitted to isolate batch-size and learning-rate interactions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results were omitted. Literature results cited from Hoffer et al. and Goyal et al. were excluded because they are prior-work findings rather than this study's experiments.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and optimizer-tuning comparisons.

Language models; momentum-based recipes; full ImageNet warm-up experiments matching the cited Goyal recipe; normalization alternatives; training extended sufficiently to match small-batch update counts. Figure-only numerical values are unavailable, which is an extraction limitation rather than an untested claim component.
Dropout interventions and removal of dropout together with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparison with norm or margin measures.
Identifying and removing memorized training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Only V5 is tested. The supplied text explicitly describes the relevant performance trends despite unavailable figure values. Warm-up, longer training, and BN-size dependence do not warrant limits_scope labels because V5 already allows recipe adaptations and workload-dependent thresholds. Training instability alone does not establish a generalization penalty, and the experiments do not isolate a train–test gap at matched training performance.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Language models; comparisons against small-batch settings at identical epoch budgets for every reported configuration; some numerical values are figure-only.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measured properties tracking the generalization gap.

relation.reason: The study's own controlled batch-size experiments directly test V5.

tranche.reason: Direct batch-size sweeps measure held-out accuracy at fixed epoch budgets, matching V5's method and measure; the learning-rate reformulation is mathematically equivalent to linear scaling.

source_check.notes: Accuracy is the median over the final five epochs; Figure 12 averages two runs. R14–R16 inherit budgets of 82, 164 and 90 epochs respectively; warm-up findings are from CIFAR, and the learning-rate formulation is equivalent to linear scaling.

statements.correction: Section 3.1: ImageNet ResNet-50; 90 epochs; SGD without momentum. Section 3.5: best validation accuracy at batches 16–64. Section 2.2: summed-gradient formulation equivalent to linear learning-rate scaling. Section 3.4: warm-up experiments reported for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 ResNet-32. Section 3.6: SGD and BN batch sizes varied separately. No matched ImageNet warm-up replication reported.
statements.problem: The reported comparison is supported, but the paper does not explicitly declare a full ImageNet replication of Goyal's warm-up recipe untested; that is inferred from its reported experiments.

reader_labels.condition: Fixed epoch budgets across the reported CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet experiments
reader_labels.reason: Smaller batches generally yield better test performance; larger batches often degrade, and usable stable learning-rate ranges shrink as batch size grows (R1–R10, R13–R16, R19).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Gradual warm-up and longer training on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
reader_labels.reason: Warm-up improves large-batch results and good CIFAR-10 results extend to m = 128, while increased training helps large batches; however, best results remain with smaller batches and large-batch results remain inferior (R11, R12, R17, R18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Batch normalization batch size varied separately from overall SGD batch size
reader_labels.reason: Performance depends on both batch sizes; reducing the overall SGD batch helps, and best BN batch sizes differ by dataset (R14–R16).
